form.label: Exposure
form.description: Which open findings the network can actually reach, and which of them sit inside containers.

div.b: Reachability re-orders work. It does not remove any.
div.span: Every finding on this page is still a real vulnerability. What this page adds is the one thing EPSS and the KEV catalogue cannot know: whether this copy is answering the network. A package with no listening port is not safe — it is reached by something other than a socket, or by an attacker who is already inside — but it is not the thing to fix tonight. Nothing here is ever coloured green, because nothing here is finished. Read a quiet row as "later", never as "no".

This page opens with all matches rather than high-confidence ones only. What listens on a port is usually a compiled binary, and a binary is exactly what this app matches least confidently — it can tell that a Go executable is serving and still be unsure which module versions are inside it. Filtering those out would empty the reachable rows and hide the finding you came for, so they are shown and labelled instead: check the Confidence column before you act on one.

panel.title: What to do first — open findings by reach and by exploit likelihood

search.query: | `riskability_reachability_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | stats count AS findings BY exploit_class, reach_class, tier | fields exploit_class, reach_class, findings, tier

viz.option: Nothing to place. Either there are no open findings for this host filter, or the exposure snapshot has not run yet — see the assessment coverage panel below.

div.span: The cell holding two known-exploited findings on a wildcard port is the darkest one on the grid; the cell holding sixteen thousand unreachable ones is the coolest. That inversion is the whole point — a chart that sized by count would draw the two findings you must fix tonight as a hairline. Empty cells are drawn deliberately: a row reading zero across is a statement, and a missing row would be an ambiguity. The dashed row is not assessed — those findings are unranked because the collector on that host never reported its listening ports, so treat them as unknown risk rather than as low risk.
Click a matrix cell, a chain node or a container row to narrow the detail table at the bottom of this page to it.
This page is narrowed. The matrix and the chain stay whole so you can pick something else.

panel.title: How the network gets there — port, process, container, package, CVE

search.query: | `riskability_exposure_chain_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | eval rk_epss = coalesce(epss, 0) | stats max(rk_epss) AS rk_epss, max(is_kev) AS rk_kev, dc(cve_id) AS cves BY source, source_kind, target, target_kind | eval rk_kev = coalesce(rk_kev, 0) | eval rk_cve = if(target_kind=="cve" OR target_kind=="cve-kev", 1, 0) | sort 20000 source, - rk_kev, - rk_epss | streamstats count AS rk_rank BY source, rk_cve | eval rk_drop = if(rk_cve==1 AND rk_kev!=1 AND rk_rank > 3, 1, 0) | eventstats sum(rk_drop) AS rk_hidden BY source | where rk_drop = 0 | appendpipe [ stats max(rk_hidden) AS n BY source, source_kind | where n > 0 | eval target = n . " more in " . source, target_kind = "cve", cves = n ] | sort 5000 - cves | head 160 | fields source, source_kind, target, target_kind, cves

viz.option: No chain to draw: no open finding is behind a listening port. That is a real answer, not a missing one — check the assessment coverage panel below to be sure the ports were measured at all.

div.b: Every hop here is measured, and the picture is still not the whole route.
div.span: The collector saw the port, the process holding it and the packages inside; it did not see your firewall, your reverse proxy or your network segmentation. A wildcard bind means the process would answer any address that reaches the host — not that the internet can. Bubble size is the largest number of CVEs reachable through any single hop touching that node, so sibling sizes do not add up. Only the 160 busiest hops are drawn. A dashed node is a hole in what the collector could see — a port answering with no process attributed to it — which is a different thing from a hop that is known and harmless. Ports with no package behind them never reach this graph at all, because nothing can be matched against them; they are counted in Ports with no package below. Each package shows its known-exploited CVEs and its three highest-scoring others by name; the rest are collected into a single "N more in <package>" node rather than drawn as fifty unreadable bubbles. Only the twelve busiest nodes in a column carry a label — hover any unlabelled one to read it.

search.query: | `riskability_hosts_seen` | search hostname=$host_tok|s$ | lookup riskability_exposure_hoststate_lookup hostname OUTPUT listeners, wildcard_listeners, unattributed_listeners, packages_behind_ports, containers, assessed_at | eval status = if(isnull(assessed_at), "never reported a listening port", "assessed") | eval assessed = if(isnull(assessed_at), "never", strftime(assessed_at, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")) | eval listeners = coalesce(listeners, 0), wildcard_listeners = coalesce(wildcard_listeners, 0), unattributed_listeners = coalesce(unattributed_listeners, 0), packages_behind_ports = coalesce(packages_behind_ports, 0), containers = coalesce(containers, 0) | table hostname, status, assessed, listeners, wildcard_listeners, unattributed_listeners, packages_behind_ports, containers | sort 5000 status, - wildcard_listeners | rename hostname AS "Host", status AS "Exposure", assessed AS "Measured at", listeners AS "Ports", wildcard_listeners AS "Any-address ports", unattributed_listeners AS "Ports with no package", packages_behind_ports AS "Packages", containers AS "Containers behind ports"

viz.option: No hosts have reported inventory yet.

div.b: A host that never reported ports is not a host with no ports.
div.span: Older collectors report inventory but no exposure. Their findings land in the not assessed row of the matrix rather than in the calm one, so that a fleet does not look safer for being less well instrumented. "Ports with no package" is the other honest gap: something is listening and the app cannot say what code is behind it.

panel.title: Containers — a stopped container is not a safe container

search.query: | `riskability_container_findings_for($host_tok|s$)` | stats dc(cve_id) AS cves, count AS findings, dc(package) AS packages, max(epss) AS peak_epss, sum(if(isnotnull(kev_added) AND kev_added!="", 1, 0)) AS kev BY hostname, container_label, image_label, state, published, ctr_tier | eval peak_epss = round(peak_epss, 4) | sort 5000 ctr_tier, - kev, - cves | table ctr_tier, hostname, container_label, image_label, state, published, cves, kev, packages, peak_epss | rename ctr_tier AS "Priority", hostname AS "Host", container_label AS "Container", image_label AS "Image", state AS "State", published AS "Ports", cves AS "CVEs", kev AS "Known-exploited", packages AS "Packages", peak_epss AS "Peak EPSS"

viz.option: No open finding is scoped to a container. Either no containers were reported, or their images carry no matched vulnerability.

div.b: Why stopped containers are still listed.
div.span: A stopped container is one docker start away from being a running one, and its vulnerabilities are latent rather than absent. It is ranked last, not removed. A container with no published port is ranked below one that publishes: the image is identical, the reach is not.

search.query: | `riskability_container_findings_for($ctr_host_tok|s$)` | search container_label=$ctr_tok|s$ | eval kev = if(isnotnull(kev_added) AND kev_added!="", "yes", "") | eval epss = round(epss, 4) | table cve_id, package, last_version, fixed_version, severity, kev, epss, image_label, state, published | sort 5000 - epss | head 2000 | rename cve_id AS "CVE", package AS "Package", last_version AS "Installed", fixed_version AS "Fixed in", severity AS "Severity", kev AS "Known-exploited", epss AS "EPSS", image_label AS "Image", state AS "State", published AS "Ports"

div.b: These findings are the image's, not the host's.
div.span: They were matched against the operating system declared inside the container, which is often a different distribution from the host it runs on. Fixing them means rebuilding or replacing the image — patching the host will not move them.

search.query: | `riskability_reachability_for($host_tok|s$, $conf_tok|s$)` | search $reach_filter$ $exploit_filter$ | eval rk_nodes = mvappend(package, cve_id, split(coalesce(ports_text, ""), ", "), split(coalesce(listener_text, ""), ", "), split(coalesce(container_text, ""), ", ")) | search $node_filter$ | eval kev = if(isnotnull(kev_added) AND kev_added!="", "yes", "") | eval epss = round(epss, 4) | eval root = if(scope_id!="", scope_id, "host") | table tier, reach_class, exploit_class, confidence, cve_id, package, last_version, fixed_version, hostname, root, ports_text, listener_text, listener_path_text, container_text, kev, epss | sort 50000 - epss | head 2000 | rename tier AS "Priority", reach_class AS "Reach", exploit_class AS "Exploit likelihood", confidence AS "Confidence", cve_id AS "CVE", package AS "Package", last_version AS "Installed", fixed_version AS "Fixed in", hostname AS "Host", root AS "Root", ports_text AS "Listening on", listener_text AS "Held by", listener_path_text AS "Executable", container_text AS "Container", kev AS "Known-exploited", epss AS "EPSS"

div.b: Capped at 2,000 rows, highest EPSS first.
div.span: This table is for reading a selection, not for exporting a fleet. Narrow it with the matrix or the chain above, or use Findings for the full register. "Held by" is the systemd unit or the executable's name; the full path is in its own column.
